hints.text: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus tells you the derivative of $\int_a^x f(t) \, dt$ directly. No integrating is needed.
The derivative of the accumulation function is the integrand evaluated at $x$, so $g'(x) = x^2 + 1$. Substitute $x = 2$.
Substituting gives $g'(2) = 4 + 1 = 5$, so the answer is $5$.

explanation: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part 1): if $g(x) = \int_a^x f(t) \, dt$, then $g'(x) = f(x)$.
Here $f(t) = t^2 + 1$, so $g'(x) = x^2 + 1$. The lower limit $1$ plays no role in the derivative.
$g'(2) = 2^2 + 1 = 5$. Meaning: as $x$ passes $2$, the accumulated area grows at $5$ units of area per unit of $x$ — the height of the curve there.

alternativeExplanations.title: The long way, to see why it works
steps: Actually carry out the integral with the power rule: $g(x) = \left[\frac{t^3}{3} + t\right]_1^x = \frac{x^3}{3} + x - \frac{4}{3}$.
Differentiate that result: $g'(x) = x^2 + 1$. The constant $-\frac{4}{3}$ from the lower limit disappears.
So $g'(2) = 4 + 1 = 5$. The Fundamental Theorem lets you skip straight to this by putting $x$ into the integrand.
